scenes.narration: [serious] A computer worm secretly broke machines inside Iran's nuclear program.
The target was Natanz, where centrifuges, fast spinning machines, enriched uranium.
It probably arrived on a USB stick. It hunted Siemens controllers, boxes that run machines.
Then it made centrifuges spin wrong, while screens showed everything normal.
Experts say Iran replaced about 1,000 centrifuges around early 2010.
That year, the worm escaped onto computers worldwide. Security experts in Belarus were called to help.
Reports say the U.S. and Israel built it. Neither has ever admitted it. Code had become a weapon.

facts.claim: Stuxnet was designed to arrive on a removable drive such as a USB stick, targeted specific Siemens PLCs controlling uranium-enrichment centrifuges, made them spin erratically while reporting normal readings to operators
Stuxnet came to light in 2010 after an office in Iran asked Belarusian Sergey Ulasen of antivirus firm VirusBlokAda for help with rebooting computers

ISIS (Institute for Science and International Security) reported that Iran replaced about 1,000 centrifuges at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant in late 2009 or early 2010 and that Stuxnet is a reasonable explanation
The New York Times (2012) reported the operation 'Olympic Games', begun under Bush and accelerated under Obama; an element of it accidentally became public in summer 2010
It is widely believed that U.S. and Israeli intelligence created Stuxnet; neither government has officially acknowledged it

seo.title: Stuxnet: The Computer Worm That Broke Iran's Nuclear Machines
